lineShape.example: 2026-08-16 15:28:55 · COMP/1 · the assistant was ready after 1.8s
lineShape.why: Local time to the second, then the course and section when the line is about one, then a sentence in the words a teacher would use. Not a function name and not a level: the trail is read by a person deciding what went wrong, months later, and 'started preview.sh COMP 1' beats 'DEBUG runScript(preview.sh)'.

mustRecord.carries: app version, build number, process id, bundle path
mustRecord.why: The bundle path and process id are not decoration. Two copies of the app can run at once, and when they do they take turns rewriting the same working folder; two process ids in one trail is the fastest way to see it. The bundle path answers 'is this build the one I think it is' without asking.

mustRecord.carries: OS version, OS build, architecture, core count, memory
mustRecord.why: The assistant runs natively on one architecture and not the other, and the whole toolchain emulates on the wrong one. Memory decides which model tier a teacher gets. OS build number and kernel release isolate virtualization, Metal, and WinUI/WSL2 platform issues.

mustRecord.carries: bundled assistant engine and toolchain helper software versions
mustRecord.why: The assistant flags and chat template handling depend on the engine build. Static tool versions (Colima, Lima, Docker CLI, Buildx on macOS; WSL2 and container tools on Windows) isolate whether a machine is running on expected helper versions.

mustRecord.carries: the folder path, redacted
mustRecord.why: Almost every question about a course begins with which folder it is in - and a folder outside the home directory bind-mounts as an EMPTY folder inside the container, which is a whole class of report explained by this line alone.

mustRecord.carries: the course code
mustRecord.why: 'It broke after I changed something' is the commonest report there is, and this is the line that dates the change.

mustRecord.carries: the course code and the reason
mustRecord.why: A save that failed leaves the teacher believing it succeeded. Recording only successes would hide exactly the case worth seeing.

mustRecord.carries: the launcher and its arguments, redacted
mustRecord.why: What was actually asked for, as against what the teacher believes they asked for.

mustRecord.carries: the launcher, the outcome, and how long it took
mustRecord.why: The outcome distinguishes a failure from a task stopped on purpose and from one backed out of at a question - all three exit non-zero, and only one is a fault.

mustRecord.carries: which credential was asked for, never the answer
mustRecord.why: The first publish of a section stops behind a dialog asking for a Netlify or Cloudflare token, and a teacher who does not notice it reports a publish that 'never finished'. This line is the difference between reading that as a hang and reading it as a question waiting. The answer is a live credential and is never written down - only the name of the thing asked for.

mustRecord.carries: course, section, and which assistant
mustRecord.why: Which tier is running decides what routing accuracy to expect, and it is the first thing to establish about any report of the assistant misunderstanding something.

mustRecord.carries: course, section, and how long the engine took
mustRecord.why: A slow start and a failed start read identically to a teacher ('it just sat there'). The seconds tell them apart.

mustRecord.carries: course, section, and the reason
mustRecord.why: The one assistant failure that leaves nothing else behind - no turn, no tool, no output.

mustRecord.carries: course, section, and one line the engine itself printed - shortened, and redacted like every other line on the trail
mustRecord.why: Until this existed a report from a teacher whose assistant was misbehaving could carry nothing the engine had said, because both its streams went to the null device. That was not laziness: a redirected pipe nobody drains fills up and blocks the engine mid-request, which is exactly what wedged the Windows server, so the output must never be read on the engine's timetable. It goes to a FILE, and a bounded tail of it is sampled onto the trail - never the firehose. What is sampled is deliberately narrow, and the narrowness was measured against a real engine: a healthy start prints six warnings that are pure noise here (a CORS block that cannot matter on a loopback-only server, and a token-type quirk in the weights), so warnings are NOT recorded. Errors are, along with any line naming an error or an exception - which is the shape of the two lines worth having, 'request (20030 tokens) exceeds the available context size' and 'got exception'. When the engine never becomes ready at all, the tail is taken whatever it says, because then every line is the diagnosis.

mustRecord.carries: course, section, and the sentence the teacher typed, on its own marked line
mustRecord.why: Recorded the moment the teacher's words are ACCEPTED, above every branch below it - not when the message goes to the model, and not when an answer comes back. Two different bugs came from placing it lower: a sentence matching a fixed shape returns early and never reaches the model, so a whole class of input left no trace at all; and an engine that failed, or one still thinking when the teacher gave up, lost the sentence that caused the trouble. It is also what the report's checkbox keys off, so recording it late made the checkbox vanish for somebody who had plainly just used the assistant. The general rule: record what the teacher did where they did it, above every branch, never at a later point that can be skipped.

mustRecord.carries: course, section, and the tool it ran
mustRecord.why: Some phrasings are matched in code and never reach the model at all. Without this line, 'why did it not think about what I said?' is unanswerable - the trail would show a tool running with nothing between it and the teacher's sentence.

mustRecord.carries: course, section, the tool name, the ARGUMENT NAMES, the seconds, the completion-token count, and whether it waited for the approval button
mustRecord.why: Routing has no automated gate anywhere in this product, so the field is the only place a routing regression shows. Argument NAMES rather than values: which tool with which arguments filled in answers the routing question completely, while the values are the teacher's page titles. The token count is the honest check on thinking having been switched back on - the engine parses the thinking OUT of the content, so a bad reply looks clean and is merely slow.

mustRecord.carries: course, section, and the reason
mustRecord.why: The failure that leaves nothing else behind: no tool, no turn, no output. Without this line 'I asked it something and nothing happened' is unfalsifiable.

mustRecord.carries: which assistant the teacher is set to use
mustRecord.why: The settings panel is where a teacher changes how much of their Mac the assistant may take, and 'it got slow last week' is a report about a change nobody else can date. Recording the state on the way IN also means a trail shows what the setting was even when the teacher looked and changed nothing.

mustRecord.carries: which assistant was chosen, and which one that lands on for this Mac
mustRecord.why: The choice is the single biggest lever a teacher has over the assistant's accuracy AND over the machine's memory, so almost every later report about either is explained by this line. Both halves are recorded because 'chose automatic' does not answer the question anybody is asking months later - the resolved answer depends on the Mac and on a rule that can change.

mustRecord.carries: which assistant, and how big the download is
mustRecord.why: Gigabytes over a school connection, and the commonest failure is that it never finished. A start with no matching finish is the whole diagnosis, and it cannot be seen without recording the start.

mustRecord.carries: which assistant, and how big the download was
mustRecord.why: The other half of the pair above. It also dates when a Mac gained several gigabytes, which is the answer to a disk-space question that otherwise looks like it has nothing to do with Plantoir.

mustRecord.carries: which assistant, and the reason it failed
mustRecord.why: Same reasoning as 'settings could not be saved': recording only the successes hides exactly the case worth seeing. A captive portal answers 200 with something that is not a model, so the failure here is a wrong-size file rather than a network error, and that sentence is worth having verbatim.

mustRecord.carries: which assistant, and how much space it freed
mustRecord.why: Removing one is allowed even when it is the one in use - the next time the assistant is opened it offers to download it again. Without this line that re-download looks like the app losing a file on its own, which is a report about a bug that is not there.

mustRecord.carries: which assistant
mustRecord.why: A start with no ending line reads as a stall, and a stall is what somebody would go looking for. Recording the stop is what makes the absence of a stop mean something - it turns 'started, nothing after' from ambiguous into a genuine finding.

mustRecord.carries: whether the assistant now asks before changing anything
mustRecord.why: Turning off the confirmation step changes what every later request DOES - it goes straight through instead of stopping for a button. A report that says 'it just did it without asking' is explained entirely by this line, and without it the behaviour looks like a bug in the gate rather than a setting somebody chose.

mustRecord.carries: which course, the section when the repair is about one, and what was put back — "put the front page back"
mustRecord.why: A different event from finding the problem, deliberately: one records that something is wrong, the other that somebody acted on it, and a trail that could not tell them apart leaves "did they ever fix it?" unanswerable. Only the two genuinely repairable cases can produce it — a missing Media folder and a missing section front page.

mustRecord.carries: which course and section, and a sentence naming what happened with the stable check NAME in brackets — 'found a problem with this course’s folders (curriculumCoverageFoundNothing)'. Never the product wording, which changes, and never anything written on a page
mustRecord.why: A teacher who reports 'it stopped showing my curriculum map last month' leaves nothing to look at otherwise: the finding is printed into a build console that is gone by then, and the condition itself is invisible on disk — a renamed folder looks exactly like a folder that was always called that. Recording the check NAME rather than the sentence is deliberate: the sentence is product wording and will be reworded, while the name is what a person searching the trail six months later can match against the contract.

mustRecord.carries: which section, and which destinations it was published to
mustRecord.why: Why a section stopped saying " — Edited". The marker is DERIVED - its presence and its absence look identical on disk - so a teacher reporting 'it still says Edited after I published' leaves nothing to look at without this line. It is also the only record that a publish succeeded at EVERY destination rather than merely at one.

mustRecord.carries: the course code, the scope ('shared' or 'per-section'), and the item name
mustRecord.why: A teacher removed a folder or file in Course Settings, excluding it from previews and deploys. Without this line, 'why is my folder not showing on the site' cannot be answered from the trail alone.

mustRecord.carries: the course code, the scope ('shared' or 'per-section'), and the item name
mustRecord.why: A teacher added back a previously excluded folder or file in Course Settings, returning it to previews and deploys.

mustRecord.carries: the item name, which list it is in, and the reason sentence the teacher was shown (a specialNames sentence, never page content)
mustRecord.why: A teacher tried to remove or untick a folder or file a feature depends on (Course Settings or the New Course Wizard) and was shown why it cannot go. 'I could not remove the folder' is a report support will receive; the line says which rule refused.

mustRecord.carries: the course code, the old folder name, the new one, which list it was in, and how many folders on disk were moved
mustRecord.why: A rename leaves nothing behind to look at: a folder called 'Class Pages' is indistinguishable from one that was always called that, and every key that named the old one has been rewritten. Without this line, 'when did this course stop having a Tasks folder?' — the first question asked when a curriculum map goes wrong — has no answer at all. The folder NAME is recorded; nothing from inside the folder ever is.

mustRecord.carries: the course code, the folder name, and which list it was added to
mustRecord.why: Adding a name in Course Settings now creates the folder on disk, so a folder appears in the teacher's vault that they did not make in Obsidian. Separate from the rename because it answers a different question, and unexplained new folders are exactly what a teacher reports as 'Plantoir did something to my notes'.

mustRecord.carries: the service's name and the folder path, redacted — recorded by a WINDOW only, never by the assistant's or the MCP server's own reading of a folder, since those show nothing
mustRecord.why: The working folder just opened is kept in sync by a cloud service and the teacher had not yet been told about THIS folder. The effects of a synced folder — a slow build, a rename that takes minutes, a move that failed once — arrive weeks later as unrelated reports, and this one line is what connects them. See cloudSyncedFolders.

mustRecord.carries: whether it was the picker's choice or the window's notice, and the service's name
mustRecord.why: The teacher read the note and went ahead. Separate from 'synced folder noticed' because it is a different fact: one says Plantoir saw it, the other says the teacher did — and 'nobody warned me' is answered by the second, not the first.

mustRecord.carries: the course code
mustRecord.event: built site moved out of the working folder
mustRecord.line: moved {course}'s built website out of the working folder, so it is no longer copied, synced or backed up with the course
mustRecord.lineWhy: The one line in this list whose WORDS are pinned, because it has two authors: the app writes it when a folder is opened, and the launchers write it when the move is done by a build at the command line or by a publish launchd ran overnight. A sentence typed in two places is a sentence that stops matching, and a trail whose lines differ by who wrote them is one nobody can search.
mustRecord.why: A one-off change a teacher can SEE. Their working folder suddenly weighs much less, a folder they may have looked at in Finder is a shortcut afterwards, and a folder they sync stops uploading builds. Each of those arrives separately — 'where has my website gone?', 'did something delete my files?', 'why did my folder shrink?' — and this line, dated and per course, answers all three. Recorded ONCE per course, at the moment the move happens, and never again: a line on every launch would say nothing and bury the one that does.
mustRecord.appliesOnWhy: Windows has always built into %LOCALAPPDATA%\Plantoir\builds\<id> (PLANTOIR_BUILD_ROOT, row 290), so there is nothing to move there and no moment to record. If Windows ever migrates a folder that predates that, the event is here to use.

mustRecord.carries: which course and section, and HOW MANY website-builder processes were ended
mustRecord.why: The count is the point. Stopping a preview, closing a window or cancelling a publish asks the launcher to end whatever that section still has running, and nothing else on the trail can tell “there was nothing left to stop” from “a build was still going and was ended” — which are the two competing explanations when a teacher reports that their publish stopped halfway. Recorded from 2026-09-05, when the sweep began ending a mid-flight BUILD and its driver rather than only a preview server: that is a change in what a teacher can lose, and it had no line describing it. The launcher prints the number and the app used to discard it.

activityTrail.note: The breadcrumb trail: what the teacher was doing, in the order they did it, in ONE file. Task records answer 'what did that publish print'; they do not answer the question support opens with, which is 'what were you doing when it went wrong'. Two files each holding half a story force whoever reads them to interleave by timestamp in their head, and they will get it wrong - so the assistant's turns go in here too. The list below is the MINIMUM: an app may record more, but a missing event is a gap in both apps at once. Deliberately coarse - every line is something a teacher would recognise as an action they took, never a view redraw or a state change, because the failure mode of logging everything is that the one line that mattered is on page forty.

promptMarker.why: The teacher's own words go on their own line behind a fixed prefix, so leaving them out of a report is dropping lines by prefix rather than parsing anything. They are kept locally because a routing problem cannot be looked into without the sentence that caused it, and withheld from the report unless the teacher ticks the box, because their words are the one thing here unmistakably theirs to hand over.

activityTrail.rule: EVERY new feature, and every CHANGED behaviour, that a teacher can see leaves a line on this trail. Adding one means naming the event here and in both apps — not writing free text at a call site, and not deciding it is too small to bother with. The failure this prevents is the one already met in the field: a teacher builds a preview, opens the assistant, asks for a report, and is told there is nothing to report, because the two things they just did were not among the things anybody had thought to record. A feature that leaves no trace is a feature that can only be diagnosed by asking the teacher to do it again, which is the thing they came to you because they could not do.

assistantConfirmation.note: Whether the assistant describes what it is about to do and waits for a button, before anything that changes the built website.
assistantConfirmation.why: The local model is a router and routers are wrong sometimes. Showing what it understood before it acts turns a misroute from a thing that HAPPENS into a thing a teacher declines.

sameOnBothAssistants.why: The smaller assistant used to refuse to be turned off and was never told the setting existed, on the measured reasoning that one request in five going wrong is not a rate at which anybody should stop reading. That withheld a setting from exactly the machine where knowing about it matters most. The measured number is put in front of the teacher as a caution instead, which respects the measurement AND the person.

deployingAlwaysAsks.why: Deploying puts work in front of students and cannot be taken back by us, so it is gated separately and the setting does not reach it.

mentionedAfter.why: For DISCOVERABILITY, not to ask for trust: a switch nobody knows about might as well not exist. App-wide because the count used to reset with every conversation, so a teacher working in short bursts could accept a hundred plans and never be told. Once ever, because a suggestion declined is an answer and asking again is how a helpful mention becomes nagging.

aCancelDoesNotResetTheCount.why: The number measures how much of the assistant's work this teacher has READ, and a cancel is evidence of reading rather than evidence against it.

oneStoredAnswer.why: The switch in Settings and the gate in the conversation are the same value, read fresh each turn - the two windows are open at the same time, and a teacher who turns it off expects the next thing they ask to go straight through.

assistantModelChoice.note: Which assistant runs on a teacher's machine, and what they are allowed to do about it. Shared because these are rules with inputs and outputs, not pictures: the panel that holds them looks nothing alike on the two platforms and must BEHAVE identically. What is deliberately not here is the layout, the keyboard shortcut, and where the settings window lives - see WINDOWS-HANDOFF.md, 'Letting a teacher choose which assistant runs'.

automaticResolvesAtPointOfUse.why: The automatic choice is stored as an INTENT and resolved every time it is used, never resolved once and written into preferences. Storing the answer would mean a later change to the tier ladder reached every machine EXCEPT the ones whose teacher had opened Settings - so the people who engaged with the setting would get the stalest behaviour.

comfortFraction.why: A model is comfortable on a machine when its resident size is at most a third of physical memory. Not a new number: it is the line the automatic ladder has always been held to, which is why the automatic choice can never produce a caution and a test asserts that.

caution.appearsWhen: a hand-picked choice is not comfortable on this machine
mustName: the chosen assistant's memory while working
caution.why: A caution rather than a disabled row. A teacher who has just quit everything else knows something the operating system does not, and greying the option out with the reason beside it gives them no way to act on what they know. What they are owed is both numbers in one sentence, so the choice is informed rather than prevented.

removal.why: The refusal is about ANY open assistant, not about whether that window happens to use that rung: working out which file is genuinely mapped means tracking state neither app keeps, and getting it wrong deletes weights out from under a running engine. Removing the CHOSEN one is allowed on purpose - it is not a broken state, it is the state every machine is in before its first download, and refusing would trap a teacher who wants their disk space back behind a choice they did not want to change.

guidance.why: Two different decisions, and neither is guessable from the other: disk is what runs out on a small laptop, memory is what makes the machine feel slow while a class is being prepared and never appears as a number anywhere. On the mac the larger download is 2.2x the smaller but 2.9x the memory, because most of the difference is the conversation being held rather than the file being read. Derive both from the tier table; typing them into the interface guarantees they drift the first time a quant changes.

namesNoModel.why: Rule one, applied where it is hardest: the settings panel is the one screen genuinely ABOUT the model, so a name leaks in most naturally here. Sweep every label, detail, caution and summary the panel can produce against this list rather than spot-checking.

cases.why: The anchor is machinery and is cut.

cases.body: Compare two designs ^ and contrast them
cases.expect: Compare two designs ^ and contrast them
cases.why: Only a BARE word can be an anchor. Anything with a space after it is the teacher's own prose, and cutting there would lose wording.

expectationWording.note: What an expectation page SAYS: the body after the frontmatter, without the `^anchor` Obsidian puts on the end of a block.

cases.why: The normal case outside the example content — folders are rarely called plain 'Curriculum'.
Case-insensitive.
The FILE name is ignored — a lesson that mentions the word is not curriculum material.

isCurriculumPage.note: Matches `build_site.py`'s own rule exactly, and that is the point — the Python decides what ships, so an app that disagreed would report coverage for pages the site does not treat as curriculum. Any FOLDER segment containing 'curriculum', case-insensitive; the FILE name is ignored.

cases.why: Either case.
BC Applied Design competency code.
BC Content knowledge standard code.
A strand heading, not an expectation.
Whole-name match: anything after the code makes it not a code.
Must start with a letter.

isExpectationCode.note: A leaf expectation is coded like A1.1 or B2.3: one letter, digits, a dot, digits — the WHOLE name, not a prefix. Index and strand-heading pages sit in the same folder and must not be counted.

curriculumRules.note: What counts as a curriculum expectation. Written after checking the code rather than from memory: an expectation is not a code found in a page's TEXT, it is a PAGE named by a code inside a curriculum folder. A first draft of this contract asserted text-scanning and was wrong before it was ever run.

followingLinks.note: What publishing and unpublishing do to the pages a named page LINKS TO. The two verbs are not mirror images and each rule is written once. Shared because both apps sweep the same folders and a difference here silently changes what students can see.

publishing.why: Publishing a page whose links lead somewhere students cannot see is the one thing publishing must never do, so it always takes what it links to, and what those link to in turn. The plan names every page that will become visible, so a teacher agreeing to publish one class can see the four pages going with it.

unpublishing.why: 'X still links to it' is a reason to keep a page published only when students can SEE X. Counting hidden referrers left pages visible and reachable from nothing, held up by drafts nobody had published - kept alive by a page that is not there. Safe in one direction because of the other: publishing is transitive, so a page taken down here comes back the moment anything visible needs it again.

neverTakenDownByFollowingLinks.kind: a page this section's Key Links points at, and the Key Links page itself
neverTakenDownByFollowingLinks.why: A section cannot do without them; they are the way in to everything else.

neverTakenDownByFollowingLinks.kind: a folder's landing page - index.md - which includes All Classes and every sidebar folder
neverTakenDownByFollowingLinks.why: It is the way IN to a folder rather than a page anything links to, so following links must never take it down.

neverTakenDownByFollowingLinks.kind: a curriculum page: any page with a folder segment containing 'curriculum'
neverTakenDownByFollowingLinks.why: build_site.py's own rule, so a course whose folder is called 'Ontario Curriculum' is covered exactly as a plain one is. In a real course this is every expectation page, the folder's own index, and the page explaining them.

theOrderIsLoadBearing.why: The exclusions are checked BEFORE the referrer test, so narrowing what counts as a referrer cannot reach them. Narrowing a sweep rule makes every exclusion above it matter more than it did the day before, which is why the exclusions are the thing to re-test after any change to what gets swept.

note: Eight rule sets that both apps need and neither platform owns. The MECHANISMS behind several of them differ completely - launchd against Task Scheduler, AppKit against WinUI, ~/Library/Logs against %LOCALAPPDATA% - which is exactly why the rules are written here instead: what must be refused, matched, stripped, or taken out of a problem report does not change with the machinery that does it.

pageNaming.note: What a page is CALLED when the assistant talks about it, which is not what its file is called. Shared because it is a rule with inputs and outputs and because both apps read the same folders: a teacher told that 'index' still links to a page has been told nothing, since every folder in a course has an index.md. Reported from a real course (ADA1O Section 1).
theRule: the frontmatter title, unless it is literally 'index'
for a file called index.md, the name of its FOLDER
pageNaming.why: Copied from Quartz's own fileTrie.ts displayName rather than invented, so what the assistant says and what the site's sidebar shows cannot drift: `const nonIndexTitle = data?.title === 'index' ? undefined : data?.title; return displayNameOverride ?? nonIndexTitle ?? fileSegmentHint ?? slugSegment`. If Quartz's rule changes, follow it.

identityIsSeparateFromLabel.why: A page's FILE NAME stays the identity, because wikilinks resolve by file name and every lookup in the page graph goes through it. Only the label changes. The trap is what happens in between: a referrer remembered by NAME and looked back up resolves 'index' to whichever folder's landing page came first in the walk, which was invisible while the answer printed as 'index' and becomes a confidently WRONG folder name the moment it does not. Carry the page, not its name.

gradedFolders.note: Which folders hold work that COUNTS FOR MARKS. An expectation is "assessed" — the ring on a cell in the Curriculum Coverage map, and Ontario's requirement that every overall expectation be evaluated at least once — when a page addressing it lives in one of these. It used to be hardcoded: any folder whose name CONTAINED "task". A teacher who called theirs "Tests", or renamed "Tasks", silently lost every assessed mark on the map with nothing said.

absentIsNotEmpty.rule: An ABSENT `graded_folders` key means the teacher has never been asked, and the HISTORICAL rule applies: any folder segment containing "task", case-insensitive. An EMPTY list means they were asked and cleared it, which is a real answer and is honoured.
absentIsNotEmpty.why: This is the whole migration, and conflating the two breaks courses both ways. The exact-name rule is NARROWER than the substring one — `support/skeletons` ships a family whose folder is "Thinking Tasks", which the old rule counted and a pool of ["Tasks"] does not — so seeding every existing course with ["Tasks"] would have quietly taken the assessed marks off that course's map. Nothing is written back from a build either: the apps serialise course_config.json wholesale from their own in-memory copy, so a key a build wrote is dropped the next time a teacher saves anything in Settings.

matching.rule: A FOLDER segment — never the file name — equals a pooled name, case-insensitively, at ANY depth.
matching.why: At any depth so a teacher who files by unit inside `Tasks` does not lose credit. Never the file name, because a page is not assessed work on account of what it is called.

cases.name: not configured: the historical substring rule
not configured: a folder that merely contains the word
cases.why: Ships in a skeleton family. The old rule counted it, so an existing course must keep counting it.

cases.name: not configured: nothing task-ish
configured: an exact pooled name
configured: nested inside a pooled folder
configured: a near miss is NOT a member
cases.why: Once a teacher has chosen the list, it means what it says. This is the case that makes seeding an existing course with ["Tasks"] unsafe.

cases.name: configured: the teacher removed Tasks
cases.why: Removing a folder from the pool is the point of the feature.

cases.name: configured: cleared deliberately
the file name never counts
an explicit null is a CLEARED list, not an unset one
cases.why: `{"graded_folders": null}` reads as configured-and-empty on both platforms rather than as absent: the key is PRESENT, and the absent case is reserved for a course that has never been asked. Pinned because the two implementations agreed by accident and nothing said which answer was intended.

askAboutPromptsWhen.why: There is something to answer the question about, so the teacher gets to decide whether their own sentences travel.

A teacher who has never TYPED to the local AI assistant should not be shown a question implying they might have - the box governs their sentences, and with none recorded, ticking it would change nothing. An unanswerable choice reads as the app knowing something about them they do not recognise. This is why 'assistant asked' is recorded the moment a message is SENT: tie it to the reply instead and the box vanishes for somebody who plainly did use the assistant, which is exactly how this was first reported.

problemReportDialog.includePromptsLabel: Include what I typed to the local AI assistant
problemReportDialog.labelWhy: The LOCAL AI assistant, said in full. Plantoir will grow ways to connect a teacher's own account with a hosted assistant, and from that day an unqualified 'the assistant' is a question about the wrong thing - answered wrongly, about where their words have been. Naming it now costs three characters and saves a rewording that would have to reach both apps at once.
problemReportDialog.note: The dialog that asks a teacher what to send. The rule worth sharing is not the layout - that is per-platform - but WHEN the question about the local AI assistant appears and what the report's own note then says. The condition is the presence of PROMPT lines on the trail, not of assistant events: opening the assistant and closing it again leaves turns but nothing the teacher typed, and the box controls only the typing.

promptStates.noteSays: nothing about the local AI assistant at all
promptStates.why: Never used it, so neither an IN line nor a NOT IN line. Promising that something was left out invites the teacher to wonder what else the app thinks they did.

promptStates.noteSays: listed under NOT IN THIS REPORT
promptStates.why: They used it and left the box unticked, which is the default. Saying so is the point: it is the promise they can check by opening the file.

promptStates.noteSays: listed under IN THIS REPORT, saying they asked for it
promptStates.why: They ticked the box. The note records that it was their choice, so nobody reading it later assumes the app took the words on its own.

reportName.why: Timed to the SECOND, not just dated. Somebody chasing a problem sends two or three reports in one afternoon - before a change and after it - and a date alone leaves a pile of files that must be opened to be told apart, or that silently overwrite one another. Dots rather than colons in the time because a colon is not legal in a file name on either platform. The folder INSIDE the archive carries the SAME stamp, or two reports unzipped side by side both land in a folder of the same name and collide on the machine of whoever is trying to help.

problemReportDialog.supportEmailWhy: Taken from here rather than from a screenshot of the mac dialog, and shown as something a teacher can CLICK rather than retype. One constant feeds the dialog and the note inside the report, so the two cannot drift.

cases.why: The account name is the single most common personal detail in this output, it appears in almost every line that names a path, and it is very often the teacher's real name. The REST of the path survives, because where a course folder sits is half of most diagnoses.

The same rule in the Windows shape. BOTH apps carry BOTH forms, deliberately: a report then reads identically wherever it was made, and neither side is left with a rule the other side's tests cannot reach.
A deploy tool announces the account it is signed in as. A board email address names the teacher and often their school.

The LABEL is kept and only the value goes. A report that says a token was present and empty is far easier to read than one with a hole in it, and the label is what tells you which credential the run was using.

Both token prompts use a silent read, so a pasted token does not echo into the output today. This rule is what stands behind that: the day a prompt is written without the silent flag, or a tool prints the token back in an error, the report is still safe.
A dumped HTTP header. The word Bearer survives so the line still reads as an authorization header.
Netlify personal access tokens carry a fixed prefix, so this one is recognisable with no label beside it at all.

An account identifier is not a credential, but it names the teacher's Cloudflare account and nothing can be diagnosed with it. The flag is kept so the report still shows that an account WAS passed, which is a real failure mode of its own.

cases.expect: Paste Cloudflare Account ID: [removed: account id]
cases.why: This prompt is NOT silent, so whatever the teacher types echoes into the output. It is the one place an identifier reaches the transcript by being typed.

A run of exactly 40 token characters is the shape of a Cloudflare API token, and it goes wherever it appears, with or without a label. Exactly 40 - neither 39 nor 41 - so ordinary long words and identifiers are left alone.

THE ONE EXCEPTION, and it is worth having. A 40-character run that is entirely lowercase hexadecimal is a git commit or a SHA-1 digest, not a token, and those are exactly what a report about a build is read for. A real token being all-hex by chance is about a 1-in-10^24 event, so nothing is given up for it.

KEPT, and this is the field the report exists to carry: the image tag says which recipe the folder actually built from, and the container name says which working folder it belongs to. Redacting these would leave a report that cannot answer the first question anybody asks of it.
KEPT. A class site address is public by design - it is the thing the teacher hands to students - and it is how a report is matched to the site that went wrong.

KEPT. A sentence that merely says the word 'token' is not a secret, and turning the product's own error messages into holes would make failures unreadable. The rule needs a value after a separator before it removes anything.

problemReportRedaction.note: What is taken OUT of a problem report before it is written to disk, and - just as important - what is KEPT. Redaction happens as the file is written, never as it is sent: a report that is only safe when it leaves by the right button leaks the first time somebody opens the folder it sits in, and writing it safe is what lets a teacher open the file and see for themselves what they are about to send. The rules lean towards removing too much, because removing a build hash by mistake costs a moment of puzzlement while a surviving token costs the teacher their account - but the four KEPT cases below are load-bearing, and a redactor that swallows them produces reports nobody can diagnose from. There is no way to switch this off in a development build: a redactor that is off while it is being worked on is a redactor nobody has run.

alsoSaid.note: Not a refusal - a teacher may be deploying deliberately without them - but the plan NAMES the section's unpublished class pages before the teacher agrees. A deploy that runs perfectly at half six and puts up a site missing tomorrow's class is the failure worth catching while somebody is awake.
alsoSaid.rule: list the class pages students cannot see yet, by name

cases.name: a time that has already passed
cases.why: First, because it is the one the teacher can fix without leaving the sheet.

cases.name: a folder deploy whose folder is not usable
Cloudflare with no Account ID
cases.why: A deliberate divergence, and the reason is worth keeping. The mac's plist carries --account, so the question is asked here and answered once. On Windows the scheduled task could not be handed one, which would make Cloudflare unschedulable - if that is still true, refuse it with a sentence that says so rather than scheduling something that will fail at 06:30.

cases.name: an ADDITIONAL folder destination whose folder is not usable
cases.why: Checked after the primary's own two checks, in the same order additional destinations are deployed to (primary first, then each additional one) - a redundancy target with no valid folder would otherwise sit silently broken until the scheduled moment, exactly what asking everything up front exists to prevent. hasDeployedBefore is true here so the PRIMARY's own checks pass first and this is genuinely the additional check firing.

cases.name: an ADDITIONAL Cloudflare destination with no Account ID
cases.why: cloudflareAccountID is the SAME key the primary's own Cloudflare check uses - it is one credential per teacher, not one per destination, so a missing Account ID refuses whichever destination (primary or additional) actually needs it.

cases.name: a section that has never been deployed
cases.why: The FIRST deploy of a section asks what to call the website. Nobody is there to answer at the scheduled time and it would simply wait. Deploy once by hand, then it can be scheduled - which is what the refusal says.

cases.name: the PRIMARY has deployed before, but an additional destination has not
cases.why: The same reasoning as the primary's own check, for whichever additional destination is new - a brand-new Netlify or Cloudflare destination also asks what to call the site; local_folder never does, so it can never trigger this one. A valid cloudflareAccountID is given so THAT check passes first and this is genuinely the never-deployed check firing.

cases.name: everything in order

scheduledDeployRefusals.note: Everything a deploy running at 06:30 would ASK is asked NOW instead, while somebody is awake to answer. A scheduled deploy that stops at a prompt in the dark is the worst outcome available: it reports nothing, changes nothing, and is discovered by a class looking at yesterday's site. Checked in this ORDER - the first match is what the teacher is told, so a time in the past is answered before a missing account.

cases.why: An empty filter shows everything.
Trimmed first.

Case-insensitive, and mid-word against the NAME as well as the code — so 'ics' finds ICS3U by its code AND SPH4U through 'Phys-ics'. That looks like a bug and is the rule working: a teacher hunting for a course types more letters, and one who typed 'ics' meaning Physics is served too. This case was written expecting ICS3U alone, and running it said otherwise.

That looks like a bug and is the rule working: a teacher hunting for a course types more letters, and one who typed 'ics' meaning Physics is served too. This case was written expecting ICS3U alone, and running it said otherwise.
